items.answer: Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

Rasterization is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms continuous device coordinate descriptions into discrete pixel-grid screen descriptions by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.

The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that selects a portion of a 3D scene and transforms it from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

Viewing transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that defines the view coordinate system and maps a scene from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional view coordinate system.

Projection transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that maps objects from a three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional view plane or coordinate system.

questions.question: How do the resource requirements for realistic scene generation compare in VR and AR?
options: AR requires more resources than VR
VR requires fewer resources than AR
VR and AR require the same resources
VR requires more resources than AR
questions.explanation: Realistic scene generation is more important in VR than in AR and requires more resources in VR than in AR.

questions.question: What is the basic idea behind producing an image with the viewing pipeline?
options: selecting a portion of a 2D display and projecting it onto a 3D scene
removing hidden surfaces from a 3D scene and displaying the remaining objects
transforming the entire 3D scene directly into a 2D device coordinate space
selecting a portion of a 3D scene and projecting it onto a 2D display
questions.explanation: The viewing pipeline creates a display image by selecting a portion of a 3D scene and projecting that portion onto a 2D display or view plane. Hidden-surface removal is a separate pipeline operation, not the basic idea of image formation.

questions.question: In the described viewing pipeline, where do clipping and hidden surface removal take place?
options: in the 2D view plane
in the 3D world coordinate system
in the 2D device coordinate space
in the 3D view coordinate system
questions.explanation: The pipeline treats clipping and hidden surface removal as operations that occur in the 3D view coordinate system, not in the world, view-plane, or device coordinate spaces.

questions.question: Which description of the viewing pipeline's stage order is accurate?
options: the stage order is not fixed
the stage order is fixed by the scene
the stage order is fixed by implementation
the stage order is fixed by the display
questions.explanation: Different implementations can alter the sequence of viewing-pipeline stages, so the order is not fixed by implementation, display, or scene.

data.text: VR scene generation needs more resources than AR, so its viewing pipeline matters for efficiency. The viewing pipeline is the fourth 3D graphics pipeline stage: it selects part of a 3D scene and turns it into a 2D display image. It does this through coordinate transformations and by removing geometry that cannot be seen, although implementations may order those steps differently.
points: Realistic virtual reality scene generation is more important and requires more resources than augmented reality.
The viewing pipeline, the fourth 3D graphics pipeline stage, selects part of a 3D scene and projects it to 2D.
The viewing pipeline maps world coordinates to view, then 2D, then device coordinates using three transformations.
Clipping and hidden surface removal occur in the 3D view coordinate system in the described pipeline.
The order of viewing pipeline stages is not fixed because implementations can alter it.

questions.question: What role does the world coordinate system play in a 3D viewing transformation?
options: the reference frame that defines the view plane projection
the reference frame that defines the viewport mapping
the reference frame that defines all scene points
the reference frame that defines the view volume clipping
questions.explanation: The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which scene points are defined. The view plane, view volume, and viewport are associated with later viewing-pipeline steps rather than with the definition of scene points.

questions.question: Which set of camera parameters is used to define the view coordinate system?
options: view-up vector, projection center, and view volume
camera origin, view plane, and clipping window
camera origin, view-up vector, and look-at point
look-at point, field of view, and viewport size
questions.explanation: The view coordinate system is set up from the camera position as an origin vector, a view-up vector, and the center of interest or look-at point. View planes, clipping windows, projection centers, view volumes, fields of view, and viewport sizes are not the camera parameters used for this setup.

questions.question: Which point, together with the camera origin, is used to obtain the N basis vector?
options: the look-at point
the projection point
the view-up point
the viewport point
questions.explanation: The N basis vector is obtained from the camera origin and the look-at point. The view-up point is used for the V basis vector, while projection and viewport locations belong to later viewing-pipeline steps.

questions.question: After the view coordinate system is defined, how is a world-coordinate point converted to view coordinates?
options: by clipping its point vector against the view volume
by multiplying its point vector by the composite transformation matrix
by mapping its point vector into the device viewport
by projecting its point vector onto the two-dimensional view plane
questions.explanation: World-to-view conversion is done by translation and rotation through a composite transformation matrix applied to the world-coordinate point vector. Projection, clipping, and viewport mapping are later or separate pipeline operations.

data.text: Scene points are first defined in the world coordinate system, and the 3D viewing transformation changes that world description into a view description that simulates the camera view. To do this, camera position, view-up point, and look-at point define a view coordinate system whose orthogonal unit axes are N, V, and U. Once those axes exist, a composite translation and rotation matrix built from them transforms world points into view points.
points: The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.
The 3D viewing transformation converts world coordinates to view coordinates to simulate looking with the camera.
The view coordinate system is set up from camera position, view-up point, and look-at point.
N opposes the look direction, V follows view-up, and U is their cross product, giving orthogonal unit axes.
A view point is the world point multiplied by a composite rotation-translation matrix from the view-coordinate axis vectors.

questions.question: Which view-volume shape is used when the projectors converge at a center of projection?
options: A normalized unit-cube-shaped region
A frustum-shaped region
A rectangular clipping-window-shaped region
A rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region
questions.explanation: When projectors converge at a center of projection, the projection is perspective and its view volume is a frustum. Parallel projection uses a rectangular parallelepiped, while a unit cube is the canonical view volume and a clipping window is only one face of the view volume.

questions.question: What happens to scene objects that lie outside the view volume?
options: They are scaled into a unit cube
They are mapped to the device viewport
They are projected onto the view plane
They are discarded by clipping
questions.explanation: The view volume defines the portion of the scene that is projected, so objects outside it are discarded by clipping. Projection, canonical conversion, and viewport mapping apply to the retained scene content, not to objects outside the view volume.

questions.question: What is the purpose of converting an arbitrarily defined view volume into a canonical view volume?
options: To make the projectors converge at a point
To discard the objects outside the view volume
To simplify the pipeline computations
To place the rendered scene on the display
questions.explanation: A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube used to simplify later pipeline computations. Converging projectors describe perspective projection, discarding outside objects is clipping, and placing the scene on the display is related to viewport mapping rather than canonical view-volume conversion.

questions.question: After a point vector in view coordinates is multiplied by the parallel projection matrix, how are Cartesian coordinates obtained?
options: By multiplying the homogeneous coordinates by the homogeneous factor w
By clipping the point coordinates before the matrix multiplication
By multiplying the Cartesian coordinates by the distance D
By dividing the homogeneous coordinates by the homogeneous factor w
questions.explanation: Parallel projection produces homogeneous coordinate values that are divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates. The distance D is used inside the projection matrix, and clipping is a separate step rather than the operation that recovers Cartesian coordinates.

questions.question: What makes converting a perspective view volume to a canonical unit cube more involved than converting a parallel view volume?
options: It requires scaling with shearing
It requires projection without clipping
It requires scaling without shearing
It requires translation with rotation
questions.explanation: A parallel view volume can be scaled into a unit cube, but a perspective frustum must be changed in both size and shape, requiring scaling and shearing. Translation and rotation describe general coordinate transformations, not the extra canonical conversion for a perspective frustum.

data.text: Projection transformation explains how 3D view-coordinate geometry is prepared for display by first limiting it to a view volume. It contrasts perspective and parallel projection, showing that their different view-volume shapes are converted into a canonical unit cube to make clipping and projection easier. The matrix steps then turn selected points into homogeneous coordinates, which are divided by w to produce view-plane coordinates.
points: Projection transformation maps 3D view-coordinate objects to a 2D view plane, usually a rectangular clipping window.
A view volume defines the projected scene region, and objects outside it are clipped before projection.
Perspective projection uses converging projectors and a frustum view volume; parallel projection uses parallel projectors and a rectangular view volume.
To simplify intensive clipping, view volumes become canonical unit cubes by scaling; perspective frustums also require shearing.
Projection matrices use D; points multiply through view, canonical, and projection matrices, then homogeneous values are divided by w.

questions.question: In the graphics pipeline, how does a viewport differ from a window?
options: It is a normalized clipping volume, while the window is a device-space screen region
It is a scene-space render region, while the window is an abstract view-plane region
It is a device-space screen region, while the window is an abstract view-plane region
It is a camera-space projection region, while the window is a display-defined screen region
questions.explanation: A viewport is the portion of the final screen where the scene is rendered, defined in device space by the display origin and dimensions. A window is an abstract view-plane or normalized clipping window, not a part of the display.

questions.question: What does the coordinate pair (Vx, Vy) represent in the transformation from (Wx, Wy)?
options: The device-space screen position of the point
The abstract view-plane position of the point
The normalized clipping-volume position of the point
The three-dimensional view-coordinate position of the point
questions.explanation: The transformation outputs a viewport point, and the viewport is the portion of the final screen in device space where the scene is rendered. The window point (Wx, Wy) is the abstract view-plane input, not the screen output.

questions.question: In the window-to-viewport matrix, what do the x-axis and y-axis scale factors depend on?
options: The display origin and the display dimensions on each axis
The projection distance and the view volume extents on each axis
The viewport and window offsets on each axis
The viewport and window dimensions on each axis
questions.explanation: The scale entries are determined by comparing the viewport size with the window size along each axis. Offsets and projection parameters affect other parts of the pipeline, not the x and y scale factors directly.

questions.question: After multiplying a window point by the window-to-viewport matrix, why is the result divided by W?
options: To convert the homogeneous coordinate result into Cartesian coordinates
To transform the point back into the original window coordinates
To normalize the point into the canonical view volume coordinates
To discard the point outside the chosen viewport coordinates
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication produces a point in homogeneous coordinates, and dividing by the homogeneous factor W recovers the Cartesian viewport coordinates. This step is not clipping, normalization, or a reverse transformation.

data.text: The window, an abstract normalized clipping window or view plane, is set against the viewport, a device-space region of the final screen. The window-to-viewport transformation maps a window point to viewport coordinates using a 3×3 matrix whose scaling and translation come from the window and viewport dimensions. The window point is multiplied by this matrix, and the resulting homogeneous point is divided by W to obtain Cartesian viewport coordinates.
points: A window is the abstract normalized clipping window or view plane, independent of the physical display.
A viewport is the device-space screen portion where the scene is rendered, defined by origin and dimensions.
The window-to-viewport transformation maps a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).
The 3×3 window-to-viewport matrix has Sx, Sy from corresponding x/y dimensions, and Tx, Ty from Sx, Sy, and those dimensions.
Multiplying the window point by the window-to-viewport matrix gives a homogeneous point; divide by W for Cartesian coordinates.

questions.question: Which option best states the key difference in the geometry discarded by clipping and hidden surface removal?
options: Hidden surface removal discards geometry outside the view volume
Hidden surface removal discards geometry visible from the viewer
Clipping discards geometry occluded from the viewer
Clipping discards geometry outside the view volume
questions.explanation: Clipping removes geometry outside the view volume before projection, while hidden surface removal removes geometry inside the view volume that is occluded from the viewer.

questions.question: What do clipping and hidden surface removal have in common when they are used to reduce rendering computation?
options: They discard geometry that would not appear in the rendered image
They map the remaining geometry from view space to device space
They project every scene point onto the view plane
They define the screen region where the image will be drawn
questions.explanation: Both stages reduce work by removing geometry that is unnecessary for the final image: clipping removes geometry outside the view volume, and hidden surface removal removes occluded geometry that would not be seen.

data.text: Clipping and hidden surface removal are two ways the VR 3D viewing pipeline avoids processing unnecessary geometry. Clipping removes geometry outside the view volume before projection, reducing the vertices that must be processed. Hidden surface removal removes geometry inside the view volume that is occluded and not visible from the viewer, reducing rendering computation and supporting realistic image generation.
points: Clipping discards geometry outside the view volume before projection, reducing vertices processed and computational complexity.
Hidden surface removal removes occluded, viewer-invisible geometry inside the view volume before rendering, reducing computation and supporting realistic images.

questions.question: What is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline?
options: Projection transformation
Scan conversion
Hidden surface removal
Viewing pipeline
questions.explanation: Scan conversion is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline. The viewing pipeline is an earlier stage, while projection and hidden-surface removal are separate pipeline steps.

data.text: The preview points to the next step in the VR 3D viewing pipeline. That step is scan conversion, which is the pipeline's fifth stage.
points: The fifth stage of the graphics pipeline is scan conversion.

questions.question: How do clipping and hidden surface removal reduce computational work in realistic virtual reality scene generation?
questions.reference_answer: Clipping discards objects or portions of objects outside the view volume before projection, while hidden surface removal removes occluded objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume before rendering. This removes geometry before projection or rendering is applied, reducing computational complexity. That reduction matters because realistic scene generation in virtual reality requires more resources than in augmented reality.

questions.question: Why does converting a perspective projection view volume to a canonical view volume require more computation than converting a parallel projection view volume?
questions.reference_answer: Converting a perspective projection view volume requires more computation because it requires both scaling and shearing, while converting a parallel projection view volume requires only scaling. A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube used to simplify pipeline computations. For perspective projection, the frustum is changed in size and shape into this cube.

questions.question: How are camera parameters used to transform a scene from the world coordinate system into a view coordinate system?
questions.reference_answer: Camera position, view-up point, and center of interest are used to define three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors for the view coordinate system. The viewing transformation is then performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix formed from these view-coordinate axis vectors. A world-coordinate point vector is multiplied by this matrix to obtain its point in view coordinates.
